_activity: Pick the civic-principle sentence that names and points
intro: Name the principle from the Civic Principles card. Pick the sentence that names it, picks a side, and points to the words.

doc.source_document: Document 4 - President Andrew Jackson, veto message on the Bank of the United States, July 10, 1832
doc.source_text: It is to be regretted that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes. Distinctions in society will always exist under every just government. Equality of talents, of education, or of wealth can not be produced by human institutions. In the full enjoyment of the gifts of Heaven and the fruits of superior industry, economy, and virtue, every man is equally entitled to protection by law; but when the laws undertake to add to these natural and just advantages artificial distinctions, to grant titles, gratuities [gifts], and exclusive privileges, to make the rich richer and the potent [powerful] more powerful, the humble members of society—the farmers, mechanics [skilled workers], and laborers—who have neither the time nor the means of securing like favors to themselves, have a right to complain of the injustice of their Government. . . .
doc._pointer: Avalon Project, Yale Law School, avalon.law.yale.edu/19th_century/ajveto01.asp, checked segment by segment 2026-10-15 (the page prints single hyphens for the dashes). Bracketed glosses ours. The map v1 listed Jackson's veto from last year's 3A; this excerpt is ours, from Avalon (D-U2).

items.stem: Which principle does Document 4 speak to?

options.1: Document 4 upholds Equal Protection, because Jackson says the law should not give “artificial distinctions” and “exclusive privileges” that make “the rich richer”
options.2: Document 4 is about banks, the national economy, and who Jackson believed his veto would end up helping the most out of everyone in the country
options.3: Document 4 upholds Federalism, because Jackson vetoed a bill passed by the federal Congress that he and his own supporters strongly disagreed with

items.reason: Option 2 describes the topic but names no principle at all. Option 3 names a real principle, just the wrong one -- Jackson's words are about equal treatment under the law, not state vs. federal power.

doc.source_document: Document 7 - Chief Justice John Marshall, Worcester v. Georgia, 1832
doc.source_text: . . . The Cherokee nation, then, is a distinct community occupying its own territory, with boundaries accurately described, in which the laws of Georgia can have no force, and which the citizens of Georgia have no right to enter, but with the assent [agreement] of the Cherokees themselves, or in conformity with treaties, and with the acts of congress. . . .
doc._pointer: Worcester v. Georgia, 31 U.S. 515 (1832), opinion of Marshall, C.J.; Legal Information Institute, law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/31/515, checked 2026-10-15. Gloss ours.

items.stem: Which principle does Document 7 speak to?

options.1: Document 7 upholds Federalism, because Marshall rules that Georgia's state laws have no force where valid federal treaty law governs Cherokee land
options.2: Document 7 is a Supreme Court ruling about a dispute between Georgia and the Cherokee Nation over who actually controls their land and laws
options.3: Document 7 denies Due Process, because Georgia never gave the Cherokee a fair hearing before taking their land

items.reason: Option 2 describes the case but names no principle. Option 3 picks a real principle, but Marshall's ruling is about which government's law controls, not about fair procedure before a punishment.

doc.source_document: Document 11 - Declaration of Sentiments, Seneca Falls, 1848
doc.source_text:
. . . The history of mankind is a history of repeated injuries and usurpations [wrongdoings] on the part of man toward woman, having in direct object the establishment of an absolute tyranny over her. To prove this, let facts be submitted to a candid world.
He has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise.
He has compelled her to submit to laws, in the formation of which she had no voice.
He has withheld from her rights which are given to the most ignorant and degraded men—both natives and foreigners.
Having deprived her of this first right of a citizen, the elective franchise, thereby leaving her without representation in the halls of legislation, he has oppressed her on all sides.
He has made her, if married, in the eye of the law, civilly dead.
He has taken from her all right in property, even to the wages she earns. . . .
doc._pointer: NYS Regents, Aug 2023, Q9–10 (_PROCESSED/nysed-exams/us-82023-examw.pdf p. 6), word for word; crop unit03-0823-mc09.png.

items.stem: Which principle does Document 11 speak to?

options.1: Document 11 denies Natural Rights, because it lists rights -- property, the vote, legal standing -- that women are born with but are not allowed to exercise
options.2: Document 11 is about the women's rights convention held at Seneca Falls, New York, back in the summer of 1848, where it was first read aloud to the audience
options.3: Document 11 upholds Representative Government, because it was written and approved by delegates who had been chosen to represent women at the convention

items.reason: Option 2 names the event but no principle at all. Option 3 has the direction backwards -- the document lists a denial of the vote, not a working system of representation, and it names no such delegates.
